submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires on content words that name the who, where and when of an empirical or clinical study: calendar periods (all twelve months, seasons, weekdays, weakly years), countries, cities and their derivatives (nationalities such as British/Japanese/European, regional adjectives such as rural, eastern, northern), and human or animal study populations (patients, subjects, participants, children, nurses, rats, rabbits), together with the study-design vocabulary that frames them (study, cohort, treatment, hospitals, recruited, conducted, retrospective). It stays at zero on organisations, personal names, body parts, diseases, natural features (river, mountain, ocean), everyday objects and code, and the same token ranking holds in non-academic sentences (Spearman 0.92-0.95 across three unrelated frames), so the preference is lexical rather than a register detector.

rival_explanations: It is really only a calendar-date detector: months, seasons and weekdays are the whole trigger, and the place and population peaks are borrowed from the dated Methods sentences they sit in, so 'Kuwait' or 'patients' in a sentence with no date should not fire above baseline.

It is a topic/register detector for clinical-epidemiology prose, so the token identities merely proxy for 'this sentence is a study description' and the same words in a travel, fiction or diary register (for example 'we flew into Kuwait in January') should go quiet.

This week all the work Sarah and I have done has been accompanied by a fruit and nut brownie. Each day I have had one packed in my bag for afternoon tea, and it’s been making these days filled with too many things to do bearable. I hate being a busy person. Maybe it’s because the days are so physically short at the moment – it is almost the winter solstice – that they feel so long. We aren’t actually working until late at night, it just feels like we are because it’s pitch black at five. All I want to do is stare at the ocean. There’s something about blue water, the horizon line, and blue sky that makes everything feel right. We’ve booked in a tiny trip to look at some freezing ocean. Hopefully the sky will be clear, the days cold and shiny. Until then we have the brownies. Sarah has been playing around with the concept of the fruit and nut brownie since the beginning of the year, and last Sunday she got it ridiculously right. They’re perfectly fudgy. They have the beautiful brownie top that looks like dried, cracked mud, and the dark complexity of the prunes is a delicious surprise. Perhaps I’ll even make her pack some for the trip to the ocean. Preheat the oven to 180 C. Line the brownie pan. A shallow, rectangular tin is best. Melt the butter and chocolate together in a large heavy based saucepan. In a large bowl or jug whisk together the sugar, eggs and vanilla until combined. In another bowl measure out the flour and salt. Add the nuts. When the chocolate and butter have melted and cooled a little, mix in the egg mixture. Then the flour and nuts. When combined scrape into your prepared tin. Bake for 25mins, the brownies should still be a bit gooey. You don’t want them to be too firm as they will continue to cook while cooling in their tin. Chop into squares. Hi there- I remember you tweeted about your idea of fruit & nut brownies a while back and I went like uh-oh! excited to finally get to see them here, and oh do they look scrumptious! thanks for sharing and hope you’re coping with the long and dull melbourne autumn/winter. Hi chika! Yes, they are finally up! Sarah loves the winter, I’m the one that needs a brownie to survive. These look AMAZING, I will definitely give them a try! Fruit and nut brownie, thats what I call balance! I made these last week for work and they were the perfect mid-morning and mid-afternoon pep-me-up. They were also a great breakfast and lessert (lunch dessert)! Actually these were great at any time of the day. I am certainly making these! Might make them early next week and take some for “you know who”! Could you please provide the recipe for the fruit and nut brownies mentioned in the text material?<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant
Certainly! Here's the recipe:

Ingredients:
- 200g dark chocolate, roughly chopped
- 150g unsalted butter
- 1 cup caster sugar
- 3 large eggs
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
- 1 cup plain flour
- 1/2 teaspoon salt

Introduction

Poverty is a major public health issue affecting millions of people worldwide. Children who grow up in poverty are at a high risk of experiencing adverse health outcomes, especially mental health problems. Children living in poverty frequently experience multiple stressors associated with inadequate material resources, unsafe living conditions, and limited access to healthcare, education, and other essential services. The high prevalence of poverty in low-and-middle-income countries compromises mental health support and access to services for children. This research paper aims to investigate the effects of poverty on mental health support for children.

Effects of Poverty on Mental Health Support for Children

Poverty affects children's mental health significantly. Poverty-related stress, material deprivation, and other barriers to accessing mental health services increase the risk of children developing mental health problems. Studies have shown that children living in poverty face significant challenges that can have long-term effects on mental health outcomes. Poverty creates stress within the household, with parents often struggling to provide basic needs such as food, shelter, and clothing. The emotional and financial strain can lead to increased parental stress, which can, in turn, negatively affect children's mental health.

Poor housing conditions and overcrowding, which are common in low-income areas, are associated with poorer mental health outcomes in children. Poor-quality housing is linked to increased risk of respiratory and other physical illnesses, which can also impact mental health outcomes. Inadequate housing conditions and exposure to environmental toxins such as lead increase the risk of developmental delays and behavioral problems in children.

Children living in poverty face multiple barriers in accessing mental health support services. High levels of poverty reduce the availability, quality, and accessibility of health care services, including mental health support services. Schools in low-income areas often lack resources as well, which can reduce opportunities for mental health support. The stigma attached to mental illness and the low level of mental health literacy in low-income communities can also discourage families from seeking care.

Poverty and Mental Health Outcomes

Poverty has been linked with a range of mental health problems in children. These include depression, anxiety, and conduct disorder, among others. The lower the family's income, the higher the risk of developing mental health problems in children. Poverty can lead to negative outcomes, including lower self-esteem, poor academic performance, and social isolation, which can contribute to poor mental health outcomes in children.

His great, great, great grandson Lamech was a man as undisciplined and violent as Cain himself, and in his godless tradition. In Lamech’s own sons a godless civilisation developed; in Jabal, nomadic pastoral life, “he was the father of such as dwell in tents, and of such as have cattle”, v. 20; in Jubal, cultural life, “he was the father of all such as handle the harp and organ”, v. 21; in Tubal-cain, industrial life — he was “the sharpener of every cutting instrument of brass and iron”, v. 22 marg. readings.explanation: The pole fires on content words that name the who, where and when of an empirical or clinical study: calendar periods (all twelve months, seasons, weekdays, weakly years), countries, cities and their derivatives (nationalities such as British/Japanese/European, regional adjectives such as rural, eastern, northern), and human or animal study populations (patients, subjects, participants, children, nurses, rats, rabbits), together with the study-design vocabulary that frames them (study, cohort, treatment, hospitals, recruited, conducted, retrospective). It stays at zero on organisations, personal names, body parts, diseases, natural features (river, mountain, ocean), everyday objects and code, and the same token ranking holds in non-academic sentences (Spearman 0.92-0.95 across three unrelated frames), so the preference is lexical rather than a register detector.

It is really only a calendar-date detector: months, seasons and weekdays are the whole trigger, and the place and population peaks are borrowed from the dated Methods sentences they sit in, so 'Kuwait' or 'patients' in a sentence with no date should not fire above baseline.

It is a topic/register detector for clinical-epidemiology prose, so the token identities merely proxy for 'this sentence is a study description' and the same words in a travel, fiction or diary register (for example 'we flew into Kuwait in January') should go quiet.
